questions.title: What Is Hyperspherical Energy Really Measuring?
questions.question_body:
I read the section where you mention "hyperspherical energy" sometimes I am confused whether this quantity refers directly to neural weight vectors or activations after normalization.
For example Eq.(6) defines HE(W) = sum_{i != j} ||\hat w_i-\hat w_j||^{-1}.  Are the \hat w_i first normalised weight vectors before computing HE?
In other words do you compute cosines between raw weights or normalised ones?

questions.title: Why Does Orthogonal Transformation Preserve Pairwise Cosine Similarities Between Neurons?
questions.question_body:
Given two weight vectors \hat w_i , \hat w_j lying on the unit sphere,
guarding their cosine similarity \cos\theta = \langle\hat w_i , \hat w_j\rangle,
your method replaces each weight vector by R\hat w_i where R is orthogonal.
I would like a short argument why\langle R\hat w_i , R\hat w_j\rangle = \langle\hat w_i , \hat w_j\rangle .

questions.title: "What exactly is hyperspherical energy in the context of diffusion models?"
questions.question_body:
In Section 3 I see you define "hyperspherical energy" as $HE(W)=	frac12 igl( rac{d}{d-1} igr) igl(1- rac{2}{d(d-1)} igr) ...$ (cosine‑similarity based).  However I am unsure what you actually compute:\n* Do you normalize each neuron vector first before measuring pairwise angles?
* Is this metric supposed to capture semantic information because neurons live on a unit sphere?
* How does preserving HE quantitatively relate to keeping a pretrained diffusion model’s generation quality?

questions.title: "Why does an orthogonal transformation preserve pairwise cosine similarities between neurons?"
"How does Cayley parametrisation & block‑diagonal structure enforce orthogonality while reducing parameters?"
questions.question_body:
"The paper says $R=(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}$ with $Q=-Q^T$. This guarantees orthogonality yet limits $	ext{det}(R)=1$. How large a penalty does losing reflections incur?
Furthermore you introduce $R=	ext{diag}(R_1,	ldots,R_r)$ splitting into blocks.
* How many free parameters does this have relative to full‑rank $d	imes d$ matrices?
* If blocks are shared across layers, what bias do we introduce and how high can $r$ realistically get before computation becomes prohibitive?

questions.title: "What is Orthogonal Finetuning’s advantage over LoRA regarding stability and generalizability?"
questions.question_body:
"LoRA injects a low‑rank update $W=W^0+AB^T$. OFT instead applies a full‑rank orthogonal transform $W=RW^0$. Conceptually:
* Why would a low‑rank update harm semantic preservation more than an orthogonal rotation?
* Empirically Fig.~4 shows faster convergence – can you explain theoretically why rotating maintains a smoother optimisation landscape compared to unconstrained gradient descent?
